content: An ammeter is a specialized instrument designed to measure the electric current flowing through a circuit. The unit of measurement for electric current is amperes, which is the origin of the term ammeter. However, the term is often incorrectly spelled or pronounced as ampmeter or ameter. The earliest type of ammeter was the D'Arsonval galvanometer, also known as the moving coil ammeter. This device operates on the principle of magnetic deflection, where an electric current passing through a coil generates a magnetic field that causes the coil to move within a fixed magnetic field. To ensure minimal resistance in the circuit, the voltage drop across the coil is kept as low as possible. Another type of ammeter, the moving iron ammeter, uses one or more pieces of iron that move in response to the electromagnetic force generated by a fixed coil of wire, typically made of heavy gauge material. Unlike the moving coil ammeter, which is limited to measuring direct current (DC), the moving iron ammeter can measure both direct and alternating currents (AC). For measuring larger currents, a resistor known as a shunt is connected in parallel with the ammeter. The majority of the current flows through the shunt, while only a small fraction passes through the ammeter itself. This configuration allows the ammeter to measure high currents effectively. Traditionally, ammeters used with shunts are designed to have a full-scale deflection (FSD) at 50 millivolts (mV). Consequently, shunts are calibrated to produce a voltage drop of 50 mV when carrying their maximum rated current. Zero-center ammeters are used in applications where current measurements of both polarities are required, such as in scientific and industrial equipment. These ammeters are also commonly placed in series with a battery. In this setup, the needle deflects to one side of the scale (typically the right) when the battery is charging and to the opposite side when the battery is discharging. Digital ammeters employ an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) to measure the voltage across the shunt resistor. The digital display is calibrated to show the current flowing through the shunt. Due to the very low resistance of the ammeter shunt, incorrect wiring of the ammeter in parallel with a voltage source can result in a short circuit. This can lead to blown fuses, damage to the instrument and wiring, and potential injury to the user. In AC circuits, a current transformer is used to convert the magnetic field around a conductor into a smaller AC current, typically 1 or 5 amperes at full rated current, which can be easily measured by the ammeter. Similarly, accurate AC/DC non-contact ammeters have been developed using Hall effect magnetic field sensors. A portable, hand-held clamp-on ammeter is a widely used tool for the maintenance of industrial and commercial electrical systems. This device can be temporarily clipped over a wire to measure the current without requiring direct contact with the conductor. The schematic symbol for an ammeter is represented by the letter A within a circle, as shown in circuit diagrams.
